Documenting Storm Damage the Way an Adjuster Needs to See It

Piedmont summer storms bring hail and straight-line wind fast enough to damage a commercial roof in twenty minutes, and the occasional remnant of an Atlantic hurricane can dump enough rain in a day to find every weak point in an aging membrane. When that happens, the roof work and the insurance claim move on the same clock. We document damage the way an adjuster needs to see it and get buildings dried in before a manageable claim turns into a total loss.

Who Calls Us After a Storm

Sometimes it's the building owner directly, sometimes a property manager working through an ownership group's claims process, and sometimes a restoration general contractor or public adjuster who needs a roofing scope to round out a broader property damage claim. We work with all three, and we adjust our documentation to whoever is actually managing the claim file.

We also get called directly by carriers and adjusters who need an independent roof assessment on a commercial claim, separate from the contractor who may end up doing the repair.

The Piedmont sees a fairly predictable storm calendar: spring and summer thunderstorm cells that can carry hail and straight-line wind gusts strong enough to lift field membrane, occasional tornado warnings during severe outbreaks, and the tail end of tropical systems moving up from the Gulf or Atlantic coast that bring sustained heavy rain rather than wind. Each pattern damages a roof differently, and we note which one we're looking at in our report rather than defaulting to generic storm language.

What Our Damage Documentation Includes

Insurance claims move faster and get fewer supplement requests when the initial scope is thorough. Our inspection reports for storm claims include:

  • Photo documentation organized by roof section, keyed to a roof plan or sketch
  • Wind and hail damage assessed against manufacturer and industry impact-testing standards
  • A line-item scope formatted to align with standard estimating software categories
  • Material availability and match documentation where a partial repair is being considered
  • Code-upgrade items required by the current building code that a like-for-like repair would miss

Matching Existing Systems on a Partial Claim

A hailstorm rarely damages an entire roof evenly, and carriers often want to know whether a damaged section can be repaired to match the surrounding membrane or whether the manufacturer no longer produces a matching product. We check discontinued or changed material lines against the existing installed system and document that finding directly, since it's often the deciding factor in whether a claim covers a section repair or the full roof.

Where local or state building code requires a full roof replacement once damage exceeds a certain threshold, or where code-driven upgrades apply to any roof work done after a certain date, we document that requirement clearly rather than letting it surface as a dispute mid-claim.

We also note where a partial repair would leave two different membrane ages or warranty terms on the same roof, since that mismatch can complicate a future claim even when the immediate repair is approved without issue.

Distinguishing Storm Damage From Wear and Deterioration

Not every roof problem found after a storm was caused by the storm. Aged membrane, existing ponding, and prior wear patterns look different under inspection than fresh wind or hail impact, and carriers scrutinize that distinction closely on commercial claims. We document both conditions honestly in the same report, which holds up better through adjustment than a scope that attributes every deficiency to the weather event.

We describe what we find and what caused it. We do not promise a claim outcome, and we don't structure documentation to argue a result rather than report a condition.

This distinction matters most on older built-up and modified bitumen roofs, where years of foot traffic and UV exposure can produce cracking that looks similar to impact damage to an untrained eye but reads very differently once the membrane is examined directly.

Getting the Building Dry While the Claim Moves

A claim can take weeks to settle, and a roof cannot stay open that long. We move directly into emergency dry-in to stop active water intrusion, documenting that mitigation work separately so it's billed and reported as its own line item within the broader claim rather than folded into the eventual repair scope in a way that confuses the adjuster.

Once the building is dry and stable, we move into the full storm damage repair scope once the claim resolves, using the same documentation set from the initial inspection so nothing has to be re-scoped from scratch.

Questions Owners and Adjusters Ask Us

How quickly can you inspect a roof after a storm?

We prioritize storm response and typically get a roof inspected and documented within a day or two of a wind or hail event, sooner if active water intrusion is involved.

Can you document damage in a format our estimating software will accept?

We format our line-item scopes to align with the categories standard commercial estimating platforms use, which reduces back-and-forth during adjustment.

What if the existing membrane is no longer manufactured?

We check current product lines against the installed system and document material availability directly, since that finding often determines whether a section repair or full replacement applies.

Will you tell us if damage isn't storm-related?

Yes. We document existing wear and deterioration honestly alongside storm damage rather than attributing every condition to the weather event.

Can you dry in the building before the claim settles?

We move into emergency dry-in immediately to stop water intrusion and document that mitigation separately so it doesn't complicate the broader claim scope.
